At the height of Trump's trade war with China, when tariffs were being announced almost weekly, companies like Logitech immediately raised prices on their products in the US significantly.

Earlier this year, the US Supreme Court ruled these tariffs illegal and that the money must be returned to manufacturers. However, no company has yet been seen passing on refunds to consumers, and a class-action lawsuit is now seeking to remedy this situation...

The Trump Tariff Saga

Last year, Trump seized on the issue of the US trade deficit with China, seemingly believing that slapping hefty tariffs on Chinese-made products would force companies like Apple to bring their manufacturing back to the US.

Of course, that was never going to happen. The US lacks the manufacturing infrastructure, expertise, and affordable labour needed to produce consumer electronics at the scale required by major brands.

Trump kept insisting that China would pay the tariffs, but the reality is that the cost has been borne by US brands importing finished products, with the extra expense ultimately passed on to consumers through price hikes. At its most extreme, tariffs reached as high as 145%.

Take Logitech as an example. The company raised prices on roughly half of its products, by as much as 25%.

Consumers Deserve Refunds

The US Supreme Court ultimately ruled that Trump did not have the authority to impose these tariffs unilaterally, and stated that US businesses must be refunded the money they paid. The refund process is now underway.

The issue is that consumers ultimately bore the cost through higher prices, yet none of the affected companies have shown any plans to refund their customers.

The law firm CPM has filed a class-action lawsuit against Logitech in court, seeking refunds on behalf of consumers who paid higher prices during the period the tariffs were in effect.

9to5Mac's Take

The principle here is indisputable. Businesses paid the tariffs, passed the extra cost on to consumers, and now the government is giving the money back to the businesses. Morally, they should refund the relevant portion of the purchase price to consumers who bought their products during that period.

In practice, however, this will be extremely difficult to execute. Logitech would need to identify all transactions made through a vast number of third-party retailers, record what prices consumers paid, and then calculate how much of that was due to tariffs.

If this lawsuit ultimately succeeds, it could set a very interesting precedent — though it is worth noting that in class-action lawsuits, it is usually the lawyers who benefit, while ordinary consumers typically receive very little in compensation.
